Non-infectious cystitis can occur as an adverse effect of some drugs such as NSAIDs (notably tiaprofenic acid).1 Pelvic radiotherapy and some drugs used for cancer chemotherapy can also cause haemorrhag- ic cystitis (below). Other inflammatory non-infectious forms of cystitis include interstitial cystitis (see below) and rare conditions such as eosinophilic cystitis.2 1. Bramble FJ, Morley R. Drug-induced cystitis: the need for vigi- lance. Br J Urol 1997; 79: 3–7. 2. Teegavarapu PS, et al. Eosinophilic cystitis and its management. Int J Clin Pract 2005; 59: 356–60. Haemorrhagic cystitis. Haemorrhagic cystitis results from damage to the bladder wall that causes diffuse bleed- ing from the endothelial lining; damage may range from minor telangiectatic bleeding to diffuse necrotic ulcera- tion.1 Signs and symptoms include haematuria, dysuria, urgency, and increased frequency of urination. Haemorrhagic cystitis may be associated with various dis- eases, drug and radiation therapies, infections, and toxins. Associated diseases include carcinoma of the bladder, rheumatoid arthritis, and amyloidosis.1 Drugs that are of- ten associated with haemorrhagic cystitis are antineoplas- tics, particularly the oxazaphosphorine alkylating agents cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide1,2 (see also Effects on the Bladder under Cyclophosphamide, p.702). Other drugs with which haemorrhagic cystitis has been reported include penicillins and NSAIDs.2 Pelvic irradiation3 for genito-urinary malignancies may cause acute symptoms that can occur up to 6 months after irradiation; some pa- tients will develop chronic symptoms and in a small number the symptoms may become debilitating and re- fractory to conservative management. Viruses such as ad- enovirus, BK virus, and CMV can cause haemorrhagic cystitis, particularly in immunocompromised patients.1 In some cases, bacterial or fungal infection, or parasitical in- festation may be responsible.2 Other causative agents have included toxins such as dyes, insecticides, and turpentine.1 Initial supportive treatment of haemorrhagic cystitis in- volves increasing fluid intake to hydrate the bladder and dilute the concentration of any toxic agent in the urine. Symptomatic relief with antispasmodics and analgesics may be indicated.1 If haematuria does not improve or re- solve, intravesical treatment may be considered.
